title: Files and Edits — and When It Refuses

questions.prompt: You asked Claude Code to fix a typo. It shows a prompt naming the file and the change. A colleague clicks no twice and fixes it by hand. What should they have done?
options: Denied every prompt and fixed the file by hand — prompts are friction
Read the prompt, match the named action, target, and diff to what they wanted, then approve or deny and rephrase
Switched to accept-all so it stops asking
Restarted the session and asked again
questions.explanation: The prompt names the action, the target, and usually the diff; matching those to your intent is the whole skill, and it is why the tool asked at all. Option C is tempting because it removes the friction, but skipping the read is what caused the confusion in the first place. Option A gives up the tool over a question. Option D re-asks without ever reading what the first prompt said.

questions.prompt: Claude Code prints: "I can't delete files outside this working directory." There is no yes/no button. What is this?
options: A permission question waiting for an answer
A refusal — a stated constraint with no button; read the reason, then rephrase
A hint that you should say yes
questions.explanation: A refusal is text only; it tells you the constraint the tool hit and leaves you to change the request. Option A is the tempting conflation the lesson exists to undo: a question has a button, a refusal does not. Option C treats a reasoned message as a malfunction. Option D reads a limit as an invitation, which is close to the opposite of what it says.

questions.prompt: Earlier you approved an edit to `note.txt`. Now Claude Code asks before running `rm note.txt`. Why is it asking again?
options: Approval is per-action and per-scope; editing a file does not cover a shell delete of it
`rm` is on a deny list by default
Deletes always require a fresh session
questions.explanation: A yes to "edit this file" is not a yes to "run a command"; the prompt names a different tool and a different scope. Option A is tempting because it feels like the tool should generalise your yes, but the scope is deliberately narrow. Option C invents a default that the lesson does not describe. Option D has no basis — the block is the scope, not the session.

questions.prompt: You asked Claude Code to fix a typo, but the proposed change rewrites the whole sentence to "be more polite." What is the right move?
options: Approve — it understood the intent better than you did
Deny, then re-ask with a smaller scope: change "wrold" to "world"
Approve, then fix it by hand afterwards
questions.explanation: The prompt showed you a diff bigger than the one you wanted, so you deny and narrow the request — that is what reading the prompt buys you. Option A is tempting when the tool sounds confident, but a larger edit than asked for is exactly the case to refuse. Option C throws away useful state over one wrong proposal. Option D approves an edit you did not want and then cleans up after it.
